tool.name: Java
tool.tagline: Statically typed, object-oriented language for the JVM, from backends to Android
tool.description: Java is a statically typed, object-oriented language that compiles to bytecode for the Java Virtual Machine, so the same program runs on any platform. It powers a huge share of backend services, big-data systems and Android apps, with a mature ecosystem of libraries, frameworks and tools. Learning it teaches you solid type-driven design and gives you access to one of the most in-demand platforms in industry.

concepts.name: Install the JDK and run code
concepts.summary: Install a JDK, then compile with javac and run with java — or launch a single source file directly.
concepts.why: Every Java program you will ever write goes through this toolchain, so knowing what each command does saves hours of confusion.
concepts.body:
To write Java you need a **JDK** (Java Development Kit). It contains the compiler `javac`, the launcher `java`, and tools like `jshell` and `jar`. Install a Java 21 LTS build (Eclipse Temurin, Oracle JDK, Amazon Corretto and others all ship the same OpenJDK code) and check it with `java -version`.

Java source lives in `.java` files. The compiler turns them into **bytecode** in `.class` files, and the JVM (Java Virtual Machine) runs that bytecode on any operating system:

- `javac Hello.java` produces `Hello.class`.
- `java Hello` starts a JVM and runs the class named `Hello` (no `.class` suffix).

Since Java 11 you can skip the explicit compile step for a single file: `java Hello.java` compiles in memory and runs immediately. That is perfect for small experiments and scripts.

For quick one-liners use **jshell**, the interactive shell: type `jshell`, then expressions like `2 + 3` or `"abc".length()` and see the result instantly — no class or `main` required.

A few habits help from day one. Keep one public class per file, named exactly like the file (`Hello` lives in `Hello.java`). Read compiler errors from the top: the first one is usually the real cause, later ones are often follow-on noise. And when you move to real projects, an IDE (IntelliJ IDEA, VS Code with the Java extensions, Eclipse) and a build tool will run `javac` for you — but they are calling exactly these commands underneath.
takeaways: The JDK = compiler (`javac`) + launcher (`java`) + tools such as `jshell`
`javac` turns `.java` source into `.class` bytecode that runs on any JVM
`java File.java` runs a single source file without a separate compile step
pitfalls: Running `java Hello.class` — the launcher takes a class name, not a file name (or a `.java` source file).

quiz.q: What does `javac Hello.java` produce?
options: A native executable for your OS
quiz.explain: javac compiles source to platform-independent bytecode in a .class file; the java launcher runs it.

concepts.name: Anatomy of a Java program
concepts.summary: Classes, the main method, statements, comments and printing output — what every line of Hello World means.
concepts.why: You need to read the skeleton of a Java program fluently before anything else makes sense.
concepts.body:
All Java code lives inside a **class**. When you launch a program, the JVM looks for a method with this exact signature and starts there:

```java
public static void main(String[] args)
```

- `public` — callable from outside the class (the JVM needs that).
- `static` — belongs to the class itself, so no object has to be created first.
- `void` — returns nothing.
- `String[] args` — the command-line arguments, e.g. `java App.java alice 42` gives `args[0] == "alice"`.

Inside the method you write **statements**, each ending with a semicolon. Blocks of statements are grouped with braces `{ }`. Java is case-sensitive: `System` and `system` are different names.

To print, use `System.out.println(x)` (adds a newline) or `System.out.print(x)` (does not). `System.err` is the error stream, useful for diagnostics.

Comments come in three flavours: `// to end of line`, `/* block */`, and `/** Javadoc */` placed above classes and methods to generate API documentation.

Naming conventions are not enforced by the compiler but every Java developer follows them: classes in `PascalCase`, methods and variables in `camelCase`, constants in `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE`.

You may read about simplified "instance main methods" (`void main()` with no class). That is a preview feature in Java 21, so it needs `--enable-preview`; stick with the classic form for code that has to compile everywhere.
takeaways: Execution starts at `public static void main(String[] args)`
Statements end with `;`, blocks use `{ }`, and names are case-sensitive
Classes are PascalCase, methods and variables camelCase
pitfalls: Misspelling the main signature (e.g. `Main` or `string[]`): it compiles but the launcher reports that no main method was found.

quiz.q: Why is `main` declared `static`?
options: So the JVM can call it without first creating an object of the class
So it can't be overridden by subclasses
quiz.explain: static methods belong to the class, so the launcher can invoke main before any instance exists.

concepts.name: Variables and primitive types
concepts.summary: Declare variables, pick among the eight primitive types, write literals and use var for local type inference.
concepts.why: Java is statically typed: every value has a type the compiler checks, so choosing types correctly is the first design decision you make.
concepts.body:
A variable is declared with a type and a name, and must be assigned before it is read: `int count = 0;`. The compiler checks every assignment against that type, so `count = "ten";` is a compile error.

Java has eight **primitive types**, which hold plain values rather than references to objects:

- `int` (32-bit) and `long` (64-bit) for whole numbers; `byte` and `short` exist but are rarely used.
- `double` (64-bit) and `float` (32-bit) for floating-point numbers. Default to `double`.
- `boolean` for `true`/`false`, and `char` for a single UTF-16 code unit like `'A'`.

Literals have types too: `42` is an `int`, `42L` a `long`, `3.14` a `double`, `3.14f` a `float`. Underscores improve readability: `1_000_000`.

Everything else — `String`, arrays, your own classes — is a **reference type**: the variable holds a reference to an object, or `null`.

Since Java 10, local variables can use `var` and let the compiler infer the type from the initializer: `var names = new ArrayList<String>();`. The variable is still statically typed; `var` just saves typing. Use it when the type is obvious from the right-hand side, not when it hides important information.

Mark variables that should never be reassigned with `final`. Constants are typically `static final` fields: `static final int MAX_USERS = 100;`.

Watch the ranges: `int` overflows silently past about 2.1 billion, wrapping to a negative number. Use `long` for things like timestamps in milliseconds, and `Math.addExact` when overflow must be an error.
takeaways: 8 primitives: `byte short int long float double boolean char`; everything else is a reference
`var` infers a local variable's type at compile time — it is still static typing
`final` prevents reassignment; `static final` makes a constant
pitfalls: Forgetting the `L` suffix: `long big = 5000000000;` does not compile because the literal is an int.

quiz.q: Which statement is true about `var x = 10;`?
options: x can later hold a String
x is a long because var widens
var can also be used for fields
x is an int, fixed at compile time
quiz.explain: var infers the static type int from the initializer; the type never changes and var only works for local variables.

concepts.name: Operators and expressions
concepts.summary: Arithmetic, integer division, increment, comparison, logical and ternary operators, plus casting between numeric types.
concepts.why: Most bugs in beginner code come from integer division, precedence or comparing the wrong way — this lesson heads them off.
concepts.body:
The arithmetic operators `+ - * / %` behave as expected with one big surprise: when both operands are integers, `/` performs **integer division** and throws away the fraction. `7 / 2` is `3`, while `7 / 2.0` is `3.5`. `%` gives the remainder (`7 % 2 == 1`), handy for "every n-th" logic.

Mixed expressions are **widened** automatically to the larger type (`int` + `double` → `double`). Going the other way needs an explicit **cast**, which can lose information: `(int) 3.99` is `3` (it truncates, it does not round).

Shortcuts: `x += 5` means `x = x + 5` (and casts back to the type of `x`). `i++` and `++i` both add one; they differ only in the value the expression yields, so avoid using them inside larger expressions.

Comparison operators `== != < <= > >=` return a `boolean`. For primitives `==` compares values. For objects it compares references, which is why strings need `.equals` (next lesson).

The logical operators `&&` and `||` **short-circuit**: the right side is evaluated only if needed. That makes guards like `s != null && s.isEmpty()` safe. `!` negates.

The ternary operator chooses between two values: `String label = n == 1 ? "item" : "items";`.

Precedence follows math (`*` before `+`), and comparison binds tighter than `&&`, which binds tighter than `||`. When in doubt, add parentheses — readers will thank you.
takeaways: int / int truncates — make one operand a double for a fractional result
Casting a double to int truncates toward zero; use `Math.round` to round
`&&` and `||` short-circuit, so they can guard against null
pitfalls: Computing an average as `sum / count` with two ints and silently losing the fraction.

quiz.q: What is the value of `double avg = 5 / 2;`?
quiz.explain: 5 / 2 is evaluated as int division giving 2, which is then widened to 2.0.

quiz.q: In `a != null && a.length() > 3`, when is `a.length()` evaluated?
options: Only when a != null is true
quiz.explain: && short-circuits: if the left side is false the right side is skipped.

concepts.name: Strings and text blocks
concepts.summary: Work with immutable Strings: compare with equals, use common methods, build text with StringBuilder and text blocks.
concepts.why: Text is everywhere — input, output, files, JSON — and String has a few rules that trip up every newcomer.
concepts.body:
A `String` is an object holding a sequence of characters, and it is **immutable**: methods like `toUpperCase()` or `replace()` return a *new* string and leave the original unchanged. If you ignore the return value, nothing happens.

Compare string contents with `a.equals(b)` (or `equalsIgnoreCase`), never with `==`. `==` checks whether two references point at the same object; it sometimes appears to work because string literals are shared, then fails for strings built at runtime.

Useful methods: `length()`, `charAt(i)`, `substring(start, end)` (end is exclusive), `indexOf`, `contains`, `startsWith`, `strip()` (trims whitespace), `isBlank()`, `split(",")`, `repeat(n)`, and `String.join(", ", list)`.

Concatenation with `+` is fine for a few pieces. In a loop, use a **StringBuilder**, which is mutable and avoids creating a new string each iteration: `sb.append(x)` then `sb.toString()`.

For formatting, `String.format("%s is %d years", name, age)` or the instance form `"%.2f".formatted(price)` work like `printf`.

Since Java 15, **text blocks** make multi-line strings readable. They start with `"""` followed by a newline; the common indentation is stripped automatically:

```java
String json = """
    {"name": "Ana", "age": 31}
    """;
```

Inside text blocks you don't need to escape double quotes, which makes them great for JSON, SQL and HTML snippets.
takeaways: Strings are immutable — always use the returned value
Compare contents with `equals`, never `==`
Use `StringBuilder` in loops and text blocks for multi-line text
pitfalls: Writing `s.trim();` on its own line and expecting `s` to change.
Comparing user input with `==` — it fails for strings created at runtime.

quiz.q: After `String s = "hi"; s.toUpperCase();` what is s?
quiz.explain: Strings are immutable; toUpperCase returns a new string that was discarded here.

concepts.name: if, else and switch
concepts.summary: Branch with if/else and with modern switch expressions that return a value and never fall through.
concepts.why: Decision-making is in almost every method, and modern switch removes a whole class of fall-through bugs.
takeaways: Arrow-form `switch` never falls through and can return a value
Switch expressions must be exhaustive — add `default` (or cover every enum constant)
Use `yield` to return a value from a multi-statement case block
pitfalls: Using old `case X:` labels and forgetting `break`, so execution falls into the next case.

quiz.q: What does this print? `int n = 2; String s = switch (n) { case 1 -> "one"; case 2 -> "two"; default -> "many"; }; System.out.println(s);`
quiz.explain: Arrow cases never fall through, so only the matching case's value is produced.

concepts.name: Loops: for, while and for-each
concepts.summary: Repeat work with for, while, do-while and the enhanced for-each loop, and control it with break and continue.
concepts.why: Loops are how you process every item, retry operations and walk through data structures.
concepts.body:
Java has four loop forms:

- **for** — when you count: `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { ... }`. The three parts are initialization, condition (checked before each iteration) and update.
- **enhanced for** (for-each) — when you visit every element of an array or collection: `for (String name : names) { ... }`. No index, no off-by-one errors. Prefer it whenever you don't need the index.
- **while** — when you don't know in advance how many iterations: `while (!queue.isEmpty()) { ... }`.
- **do-while** — like while, but the body runs at least once because the condition is checked at the end.

Inside any loop, `break` exits the loop immediately and `continue` skips to the next iteration. For nested loops, a **label** lets you break out of the outer one: `outer: for (...) { for (...) { break outer; } }`. Use labels sparingly; often extracting a method and returning is clearer.

A variable declared in the `for` header (`int i`) exists only inside the loop. If you need the final value afterwards, declare it before the loop.

Common mistakes: using `<=` instead of `<` with zero-based indexes (one step too far), and modifying a collection while iterating it with for-each, which throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. To remove elements while iterating, use `list.removeIf(...)` instead.

Later you'll see streams, which express many loops (filter, transform, sum) declaratively. Plain loops remain perfectly idiomatic, especially when you need early exit or complex state.
takeaways: Use for-each when you don't need the index
`break` leaves the loop, `continue` skips to the next iteration
Don't add or remove collection elements inside a for-each over it
pitfalls: Off-by-one: `for (int i = 0; i <= arr.length; i++)` reads past the end and throws.

quiz.q: How many times does `do { x++; } while (x < 0);` run its body when x starts at 5?
quiz.explain: do-while checks its condition after the body, so the body always runs at least once.

concepts.name: Arrays
concepts.summary: Create fixed-size arrays, index into them, loop over them and use java.util.Arrays helpers to print, sort and copy.
concepts.why: Arrays are the low-level building block under most collections, and appear in main(String[] args), varargs and performance-sensitive code.
concepts.body:
An **array** is a fixed-size, ordered block of elements of one type. Create one with a size or with initial values:

```java
int[] scores = new int[5];            // five zeros
String[] names = {"Ana", "Bo", "Cy"};
```

Indexes start at `0`, and the last valid index is `length - 1`. Note that `length` is a field, not a method: `names.length`. Accessing an index outside the range throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` — Java always checks bounds.

New arrays are filled with default values: `0` for numbers, `false` for booleans, `null` for references.

An array variable holds a reference. Assigning `int[] b = a;` makes both names point at the *same* array, so changing `b[0]` changes `a[0]`. To copy, use `Arrays.copyOf(a, a.length)` or `a.clone()`.

The `java.util.Arrays` class has the helpers you'll use constantly:

- `Arrays.toString(arr)` — printing an array directly shows something like `[I@1b6d3586`, which is useless.
- `Arrays.sort(arr)` — sorts in place.
- `Arrays.fill(arr, value)` and `Arrays.equals(a, b)` — the latter compares contents, unlike `==`.

Multi-dimensional arrays are arrays of arrays: `int[][] grid = new int[3][4];` and `grid[row][col]`.

Because arrays can't grow, application code usually prefers `ArrayList`, which you'll meet in the collections module. Reach for arrays for fixed-size data, primitives in hot loops, and APIs that require them.
takeaways: Indexes run from 0 to `length - 1`; `length` is a field
Array variables are references — assignment shares, `copyOf` copies
Use `Arrays.toString`, `sort`, `equals` instead of hand-written loops
pitfalls: Printing an array with `println(arr)` and getting `[I@6d06d69c` instead of its contents.

quiz.q: After `int[] a = {1, 2}; int[] b = a; b[0] = 9;` what is `a[0]`?
quiz.explain: a and b reference the same array object, so writing through b is visible through a.

concepts.name: Methods
concepts.summary: Define static methods with parameters and return values, overload them, and understand that Java always passes by value.
concepts.why: Methods are how you name ideas, avoid repetition and make code testable.
concepts.body:
A **method** is a named block of code with parameters and a return type:

```java
static double area(double width, double height) {
    return width * height;
}
```

The parts are: modifiers (`static` here, meaning it belongs to the class), the return type (`double`, or `void` for nothing), the name, and a parameter list. A non-void method must `return` a value on every path — the compiler checks that.

**Overloading** means several methods share a name but differ in parameter types or counts, e.g. `print(int)` and `print(String)`. The compiler picks the best match from the argument types at compile time. The return type alone can't distinguish overloads.

**Varargs** let a method accept any number of arguments: `static int sum(int... values)`; inside, `values` is an `int[]`.

Java is strictly **pass-by-value**. For primitives the method receives a copy of the number. For objects it receives a copy of the *reference*: the method can call methods on the object and mutate it, and the caller sees those changes, but assigning a new object to the parameter has no effect outside.

Good methods are short, do one thing and have a name that says what: `calculateTotal`, `isValid`, `findUserById`. Boolean-returning methods usually start with `is`, `has` or `can`. If a method needs many parameters, that's a hint to group them into a class or record.

Local variables live only during a call. Each call gets a fresh set on the **stack**, which is also why recursion (a method calling itself) works.
takeaways: Signature = name + parameter types; overloads differ in parameters
Java passes everything by value — for objects, the value is a reference
Keep methods small, single-purpose and well named
pitfalls: Expecting a method that reassigns its parameter (`list = new ArrayList<>()`) to change the caller's variable.

quiz.q: A method does `p.setName("Bo"); p = new Person("Cy");` on its parameter p. What does the caller's Person show afterwards?
quiz.explain: The mutation goes through the shared reference; reassigning the local parameter doesn't affect the caller.

concepts.name: Wrapper types and boxing
concepts.summary: Integer, Double and friends wrap primitives as objects; learn autoboxing, parsing text to numbers and the null and == traps.
concepts.why: Collections and generics only hold objects, so you meet wrapper types the moment you store numbers in a List or Map.
concepts.body:
Each primitive has a **wrapper class** in `java.lang`: `Integer`, `Long`, `Double`, `Boolean`, `Character` and so on. Wrappers are objects, so they can be stored in collections (`List<Integer>`), be `null`, and offer useful static methods.

The compiler converts automatically between the two forms. **Autoboxing** turns `int` into `Integer` when needed, and **unboxing** does the reverse:

```java
List<Integer> ids = new ArrayList<>();
ids.add(42);          // boxing
int first = ids.get(0); // unboxing
```

The convenient conversions hide two traps:

- Unboxing `null` throws `NullPointerException`. If a `Map<String, Integer>` has no entry, `int n = map.get("x");` crashes.
- `==` on wrappers compares references. Small values (−128 to 127) are cached, so `Integer a = 100, b = 100; a == b` is true, but with 1000 it is usually false. Use `equals`, or unbox first.

Parsing text into numbers is a daily task: `Integer.parseInt("42")`, `Double.parseDouble("3.5")`, `Long.parseLong(...)`. Invalid input throws `NumberFormatException`, so validate or catch it when parsing user input. The reverse is `String.valueOf(n)` or `Integer.toString(n)`.

Other handy members: `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, `Integer.compare(a, b)`, `Character.isDigit(c)`, `Character.isLetter(c)`.

In performance-critical loops, prefer primitives: boxing allocates objects, and a `List<Integer>` of a million numbers uses several times more memory than an `int[]`.
takeaways: Wrappers let primitives live in collections and be null
Compare wrapper values with `equals`, not `==`
`Integer.parseInt` and friends convert text to numbers and throw on bad input
pitfalls: Unboxing a null `Integer` (e.g. from `map.get`) into an `int` throws NullPointerException.

quiz.q: Given `Map<String,Integer> m = new HashMap<>();` what happens on `int n = m.get("k");`?
quiz.explain: get returns null for a missing key, and unboxing null to int throws NullPointerException.

concepts.name: Console input and formatted output
concepts.summary: Read user input with Scanner or BufferedReader and print neatly with printf and format specifiers.
concepts.why: Small interactive programs and command-line tools need to read input and present results clearly.
concepts.body:
For output you already know `System.out.println`. For aligned or rounded output, use **printf**-style formatting: `System.out.printf("%-10s %6.2f%n", name, price);`.

Common format specifiers:

- `%s` any value (calls `toString`), `%d` integers, `%f` floating point.
- `%.2f` two decimals; `%8d` right-aligned in 8 columns; `%-10s` left-aligned.
- `%n` the platform line separator, `%%` a literal percent sign.

The same patterns work in `String.format(...)` and `"...".formatted(...)` when you need the string instead of printing it.

For input, the simplest tool is `java.util.Scanner`. Wrap `System.in` once and read tokens or lines: `nextLine()`, `nextInt()`, `hasNextInt()`. A classic gotcha: `nextInt()` leaves the newline in the buffer, so a following `nextLine()` returns an empty string. Reading everything with `nextLine()` and parsing with `Integer.parseInt` avoids that.

For large inputs (competitive programming, piping big files), `Scanner` is slow. Use `BufferedReader`:

```java
var in = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in));
String line;
while ((line = in.readLine()) != null) { ... }
```

`readLine()` returns `null` at end of input (Ctrl+D on Unix, Ctrl+Z on Windows, or the end of a piped file).

Command-line arguments (`args`) are another input channel; prefer them for options like file names, and standard input for streams of data.
takeaways: `printf`/`formatted` with `%s %d %.2f %n` give precise output
Reading whole lines and parsing them avoids Scanner's leftover-newline trap
Use `BufferedReader` for fast line-by-line input; `readLine()` returns null at end
pitfalls: Calling `nextInt()` then `nextLine()` and getting an empty line.

quiz.q: What does `String.format("%5.1f|", 3.14159)` produce?
quiz.explain: Width 5 with one decimal right-aligns "3.1" in five columns, padding with two spaces.

concepts.name: Classes and objects
concepts.summary: Define a class with fields and instance methods, create objects with new, and understand references, this and null.
concepts.why: Java is built around objects; every real program models its domain as classes.
concepts.body:
A **class** is a blueprint: it declares the data each object holds (**fields**) and the behaviour it offers (**methods**). An **object** is one instance created from that blueprint with `new`.

```java
class Counter {
    int count;                 // field: each object has its own
    void increment() { count++; }
}
Counter c = new Counter();     // create an object
c.increment();
```

Methods without `static` are **instance methods**: they run on a particular object and can read and change its fields. Inside them, `this` refers to that object; you need it explicitly only to disambiguate, e.g. `this.name = name`.

`static` members belong to the class, shared by all instances. Use them for utilities (`Math.max`) and constants, not for per-object state.

A variable of a class type holds a **reference**, not the object itself. Two variables can refer to the same object, and passing an object to a method passes the reference. A reference that points to nothing is `null`; calling a method on it throws `NullPointerException`. Since Java 14 the error message names exactly which expression was null, which makes these easy to debug.

Fields get default values (`0`, `false`, `null`), unlike local variables which must be assigned before use.

Override `toString()` so objects print meaningfully: Java calls it automatically in string concatenation and `println`. Without it you get output like `Counter@1b6d3586`.

Objects you no longer reference are reclaimed automatically by the garbage collector — there is no `delete` in Java.
takeaways: A class defines fields and methods; `new` creates an object
Variables hold references — several can point at one object
Override `toString()` for readable output
pitfalls: Calling an instance method on a reference that was never assigned an object, causing NullPointerException.

quiz.q: Two variables `a` and `b` reference the same object, and you call `b.increment()`. What does `a.count` show?
quiz.explain: There is only one object; both variables are references to it, so the change is visible through either.

concepts.name: Constructors and object setup
concepts.summary: Initialise objects with constructors, overload them, chain with this(...), and validate arguments up front.
concepts.why: Constructors guarantee an object starts life in a valid state, which removes whole categories of bugs.
takeaways: A constructor has the class name, no return type, and runs on `new`
Writing any constructor removes the implicit no-arg one
Chain with `this(...)` and validate arguments so invalid objects never exist
pitfalls: Calling an overridable method from a constructor — the subclass version runs before the subclass is initialised.

quiz.q: A class declares only `Point(int x, int y)`. What happens with `new Point()`?
quiz.explain: Once any constructor is declared the compiler no longer generates the default no-argument one.

concepts.name: Encapsulation and access modifiers
concepts.summary: Hide state behind private fields, expose behaviour through methods, and choose between public, protected, package-private and private.
concepts.why: Encapsulation lets you change a class's internals without breaking the code that uses it.
concepts.body:
**Encapsulation** means a class owns its data: fields are private, and the outside world interacts only through methods that keep the object valid. That way an invariant like "balance is never negative" is enforced in one place instead of hoped for everywhere.

Java has four access levels:

- `private` — visible only inside the class (including its nested classes).
- *package-private* (no keyword) — visible to classes in the same package.
- `protected` — package plus subclasses in other packages.
- `public` — visible everywhere.

The rule of thumb: start with the most restrictive level that works, and widen only when needed. Fields are almost always `private`. Helper methods are `private`. Only the operations you are willing to support long-term become `public`.

Getters and setters are common, but don't generate a setter for every field by reflex. A method that expresses intent (`account.deposit(amount)`) is better than `setBalance(getBalance() + amount)` because it can validate and it documents the allowed operations. Fields that should never change after construction should be `private final` with no setter at all.

Be careful when exposing mutable internals. Returning your internal `List` lets callers modify it behind your back. Return an unmodifiable view or a copy instead, e.g. `List.copyOf(items)`, and copy mutable arguments you store.

An object whose state can't change after construction is **immutable**. Immutable objects are simpler to reason about, can be shared freely, and are naturally thread-safe — `String`, `LocalDate` and records are all designed this way.
takeaways: Make fields `private`; expose meaningful operations, not raw state
Default to the narrowest access level and widen only when needed
Don't leak mutable internals — return copies or unmodifiable views
pitfalls: Adding a public getter and setter for every field, which is barely better than a public field.

quiz.q: A field has no access modifier. Who can access it?
options: Any class in the same package
quiz.explain: No modifier means package-private: visible to code in the same package and nowhere else.

concepts.name: Inheritance and polymorphism
concepts.summary: Extend classes, override methods, call super, and let polymorphism pick the right method at runtime.
concepts.why: Polymorphism lets one piece of code work with many types, and you meet inheritance in every framework and library.
concepts.body:
A class can **extend** one other class and inherit its fields and methods: `class Dog extends Animal`. The subclass can add members and **override** inherited methods to change behaviour. Every class ultimately extends `java.lang.Object`, which is where `toString`, `equals` and `hashCode` come from.

Mark overrides with `@Override`. The compiler then checks that you really override something; without it, a typo like `tostring()` silently creates a new method.

**Polymorphism** is the payoff: a variable of type `Animal` can refer to a `Dog` or a `Cat`, and calling `animal.sound()` runs the override of the object's *actual* class, decided at runtime (dynamic dispatch). Code written against `Animal` works for subclasses that didn't exist when it was written.

Use `super.method()` to call the parent's version from an override, and `super(...)` as the first statement of a constructor to run the parent's constructor. If you don't, the compiler inserts `super()` — which fails if the parent has no no-arg constructor.

Modifiers that limit inheritance:

- `final` class — can't be extended (`String` is final). `final` method — can't be overridden.
- `abstract` class — can't be instantiated and may declare `abstract` methods without a body that subclasses must implement.

Inheritance creates tight coupling: subclasses depend on the parent's implementation details. The classic advice is to **prefer composition over inheritance** — hold a reference to a helper object instead of extending it — and use inheritance for genuine "is-a" relationships. For shared contracts, interfaces (next lesson) are usually the better tool.
takeaways: `extends` inherits members; overriding replaces behaviour for the subclass
Calls dispatch on the object's runtime class, not the variable's type
Always write `@Override`; prefer composition when "is-a" doesn't truly hold
pitfalls: Omitting `@Override` and misspelling the method name, so the parent's version still runs.

quiz.q: `Animal a = new Dog(); a.sound();` — Dog overrides sound(). Which version runs?
options: Animal's, because the variable is an Animal
It doesn't compile without a cast
quiz.explain: Instance method calls are dispatched on the object's actual class at runtime.

quiz.q: What is true of an abstract class?
options: All its methods must be abstract
quiz.explain: An abstract class can have fields, constructors and concrete methods, but you can't call new on it.

concepts.name: Interfaces
concepts.summary: Define contracts with interfaces, implement several at once, and use default and static methods.
concepts.why: Programming to interfaces is the backbone of flexible Java design — collections, JDBC, Spring and testing all rely on it.
concepts.body:
An **interface** declares what a type can do without saying how. A class `implements` it by providing all of its abstract methods:

```java
interface Notifier {
    void send(String to, String message);
}
class EmailNotifier implements Notifier { ... }
```

A class can extend only one class but implement **any number** of interfaces, so interfaces are how Java models capabilities: `Comparable`, `Runnable`, `AutoCloseable`, `Iterable`.

The key habit is **programming to the interface**: declare variables, parameters and return types with the interface type (`List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();`, `Notifier notifier`). Your code then works with any implementation, and swapping one — or injecting a fake in a test — needs no changes.

Since Java 8 interfaces can also contain:

- `default` methods — with a body, inherited by implementations, used to evolve interfaces without breaking existing classes (e.g. `List.sort`).
- `static` methods — utilities related to the interface (e.g. `List.of`, `Comparator.comparing`).
- `private` methods (Java 9+) — helpers shared by default methods.

Interfaces cannot hold instance state; fields declared in them are implicitly `public static final` constants.

An interface with exactly one abstract method is a **functional interface** and can be implemented with a lambda — a big topic of its own coming up soon.

Interface vs abstract class: use an interface to define a role many unrelated classes can play; use an abstract class when subclasses genuinely share state and implementation. In modern Java, interfaces are the default choice.
takeaways: An interface is a contract; a class can implement many
Declare variables and parameters with interface types
`default` methods add behaviour without breaking implementers
pitfalls: Declaring parameters as concrete classes (`ArrayList`) instead of interfaces (`List`), which makes code rigid.

quiz.q: Why were default methods added to interfaces?
options: To add methods to existing interfaces without breaking their implementations
To let interfaces store per-object state
quiz.explain: Default methods supply a body, so existing implementers keep compiling when an interface gains a method.

concepts.name: Enums
concepts.summary: Model fixed sets of constants with enums that can carry fields, constructors and methods, and switch over them.
concepts.why: Enums replace magic strings and int codes with type-safe values the compiler can check.
takeaways: Enums are type-safe, fixed sets of instances that can have fields and methods
Switch expressions over enums can be exhaustive without `default`
Comparing enum constants with `==` is correct
pitfalls: Storing `ordinal()` in a database; reordering constants then corrupts the data.

quiz.q: A switch expression covers every constant of an enum and has no default. What happens when a new constant is added?
options: The new value silently returns null
Nothing; the first case is used
The switch no longer compiles until the new case is handled
quiz.explain: Exhaustiveness is checked at compile time, so the missing case is reported as an error.

concepts.name: Records
concepts.summary: Declare immutable data carriers in one line; records generate the constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString.
concepts.why: Most applications pass lots of plain data around, and records remove the boilerplate while making it immutable by default.
takeaways: `record R(A a, B b)` generates constructor, accessors, equals/hashCode/toString
Validate or normalise in a compact constructor
Records are shallowly immutable — copy mutable components
pitfalls: Calling `getX()` on a record; accessors are named exactly like the components, e.g. `x()`.

quiz.q: Given `record P(int x) {}`, what does `new P(1).equals(new P(1))` return?
options: It doesn't compile without overriding equals
quiz.explain: Records generate equals based on component values, so equal components mean equal records.

concepts.name: Exceptions
concepts.summary: Throw and catch exceptions, understand checked vs unchecked, and clean up resources with try-with-resources.
concepts.why: Robust programs must handle failure deliberately, and Java's checked exceptions force you to think about it.
concepts.body:
When something goes wrong, Java code **throws** an exception object, which unwinds the call stack until a matching `catch` handles it. If nothing does, the thread dies with a stack trace — read it from the top: the first line says what happened, the first frame in *your* code says where.

The hierarchy matters:

- `Exception` subclasses (except `RuntimeException`) are **checked**: the compiler forces callers to catch them or declare `throws`. Examples: `IOException`, `SQLException` — failures outside your control.
- `RuntimeException` subclasses are **unchecked**: programming errors or invalid input, such as `NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException`, `IllegalStateException`.
- `Error` (e.g. `OutOfMemoryError`) signals JVM-level problems you normally don't catch.

Catch the most specific type you can actually handle; combine types with a multi-catch `catch (IOException | ParseException e)`. Never swallow an exception with an empty catch block — at minimum log it.

When you translate a low-level exception into your own, pass the original as the **cause** (`throw new ConfigException("bad config", e)`) so the stack trace keeps the root cause.

`finally` runs whether or not an exception occurred. For resources such as files, sockets and database connections, prefer **try-with-resources**, which closes anything `AutoCloseable` automatically, in reverse order, even on failure:

```java
try (var reader = Files.newBufferedReader(path)) {
    return reader.readLine();
}
```

Use exceptions for exceptional situations, not ordinary control flow; for "not found" results, an `Optional` return is often clearer.
takeaways: Checked exceptions must be caught or declared; unchecked ones signal bugs or bad input
Catch specific types, never swallow silently, and chain the cause when wrapping
try-with-resources closes `AutoCloseable` resources automatically
pitfalls: `catch (Exception e) {}` — hides real failures and makes debugging miserable.
Wrapping an exception without passing the cause, losing the original stack trace.

quiz.q: Which exception is checked?
quiz.explain: IOException extends Exception but not RuntimeException, so the compiler enforces handling it.

concepts.name: Generics basics
concepts.summary: Use type parameters like List<String> and Map<K, V>, write simple generic classes and methods, and let the diamond infer types.
concepts.why: Generics give compile-time type safety to every collection and most modern APIs.
takeaways: Type arguments give compile-time checks and remove casts
Use the diamond `<>` and let the compiler infer
Bounds like `<T extends Comparable<T>>` let generic code call methods on T
pitfalls: Using raw types (`List list = new ArrayList();`) and losing all type checking.

quiz.q: Why does `List<int>` fail to compile?
options: Type arguments must be reference types; use List<Integer>
quiz.explain: Generics work with reference types only; Integer wraps int and autoboxing converts between them.

concepts.name: Lists and the Collections Framework
concepts.summary: Use List, ArrayList and List.of, iterate and sort them, and know when to pick which list implementation.
concepts.why: Lists are the most used data structure in Java code; using them idiomatically is a daily skill.
concepts.body:
The **Collections Framework** in `java.util` provides interfaces (`List`, `Set`, `Map`, `Queue`, `Deque`) and implementations. You program to the interface and pick the implementation once, at construction.

A **List** is an ordered sequence that allows duplicates and index access. `ArrayList` is the default choice: backed by a resizable array, fast `get(i)` and fast appends. `LinkedList` is rarely the right answer — despite theory, it is slower than `ArrayList` for almost every real workload. For queues and stacks, use `ArrayDeque`.

Core operations: `add(x)`, `add(i, x)`, `get(i)`, `set(i, x)`, `remove(i)` or `remove(obj)`, `size()`, `isEmpty()`, `contains(x)`, `indexOf(x)`.

Create small fixed lists with `List.of("a", "b")`. These are **unmodifiable**: `add` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, and they reject `null` elements. When you need a mutable copy, write `new ArrayList<>(List.of(...))`.

Sorting: `list.sort(Comparator.naturalOrder())` or with a comparator built from key extractors:

```java
people.sort(Comparator.comparing(Person::lastName).thenComparing(Person::age));
```

To remove elements matching a condition, use `list.removeIf(x -> x.isBlank())` rather than removing inside a for-each loop, which throws `ConcurrentModificationException`.

Watch `remove` on a `List<Integer>`: `list.remove(1)` removes the element at **index** 1, while `list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1))` removes the value 1.

Since Java 21, `List` is a `SequencedCollection`, giving `getFirst()`, `getLast()`, `removeLast()` and `reversed()`.
takeaways: Declare `List<T>`, construct `ArrayList` — it's the right default
`List.of` is unmodifiable and null-hostile; copy into `ArrayList` to mutate
Sort with `Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...)`; filter out with `removeIf`
pitfalls: Calling `remove(int)` on a `List<Integer>` when you meant to remove a value.

quiz.q: What happens on `List.of(1, 2).add(3)`?
options: It returns false and does nothing
quiz.explain: List.of returns an unmodifiable list; mutating methods throw UnsupportedOperationException.

concepts.name: Maps, Sets and equals/hashCode
concepts.summary: Store key-value pairs in HashMap, unique items in HashSet, and implement equals and hashCode correctly for your keys.
concepts.why: Lookups by key and de-duplication are everywhere, and broken equals/hashCode is one of the most common subtle bugs.
concepts.body:
A **Map** associates keys with values; each key appears at most once. `HashMap` is the default: average constant-time `put` and `get`, no ordering. `LinkedHashMap` keeps insertion order, and `TreeMap` keeps keys sorted.

Idiomatic map code uses the newer methods instead of check-then-act sequences:

- `getOrDefault(key, fallback)` — avoid nulls for missing keys.
- `merge(word, 1, Integer::sum)` — counting in one line.
- `computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(value)` — grouping into lists.
- Iterate with `for (var e : map.entrySet())` and use `e.getKey()`, `e.getValue()`.

A **Set** holds unique elements. `HashSet` is the default, `LinkedHashSet` preserves insertion order, `TreeSet` keeps elements sorted. `set.add(x)` returns `false` if `x` was already present.

Both hash-based structures depend on two methods every object inherits from `Object`. The contract: if `a.equals(b)` then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()`. The hash code picks a bucket, `equals` confirms the match. If you override `equals` but not `hashCode`, two "equal" keys land in different buckets and lookups mysteriously fail.

The easiest way to get both right is to use a **record** or `String` as a key. For a regular class, generate them with your IDE or use `Objects.equals` and `Objects.hash`.

Never mutate an object in a way that changes its hash code while it is a key in a map or member of a set — it becomes unreachable. Immutable keys avoid this entirely.

`Map.of(...)` and `Set.of(...)` create small unmodifiable collections, and `Set.of` rejects duplicate elements.
takeaways: HashMap/HashSet are the defaults; Linked* keep insertion order, Tree* keep sorted order
Use `merge`, `computeIfAbsent` and `getOrDefault` instead of check-then-put
Equal objects must have equal hash codes — records do this for you
pitfalls: Overriding `equals` without `hashCode`, so equal keys aren't found in a HashMap.
Mutating a key after inserting it into a HashMap or HashSet.

quiz.q: A class overrides equals but not hashCode. What typically happens with `set.contains(equalCopy)` on a HashSet?
options: Usually false, because the copy hashes to a different bucket
quiz.explain: Without a matching hashCode the lookup checks the wrong bucket and never calls equals on the stored element.

concepts.name: Lambdas and functional interfaces
concepts.summary: Pass behaviour as values with lambdas and method references, and use the standard functional interfaces in java.util.function.
concepts.why: Modern Java APIs — collections, streams, CompletableFuture, comparators — all take lambdas.
concepts.body:
A **lambda** is a compact way to implement a **functional interface**: an interface with exactly one abstract method. Instead of an anonymous class, you write just the parameters and the body:

```java
Comparator<String> byLength = (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.length(), b.length());
Runnable task = () -> System.out.println("tick");
```

Parameter types are inferred from the target interface. A single parameter needs no parentheses (`s -> s.isBlank()`), and a multi-line body uses braces with an explicit `return`.

`java.util.function` provides the standard shapes, so you rarely need to declare your own:

- `Function<T, R>` — takes T, returns R (`apply`).
- `Predicate<T>` — takes T, returns boolean (`test`).
- `Consumer<T>` — takes T, returns nothing (`accept`).
- `Supplier<T>` — takes nothing, returns T (`get`).
- `BiFunction<T, U, R>`, `UnaryOperator<T>`, `BinaryOperator<T>`, plus primitive variants like `IntPredicate` that avoid boxing.

A **method reference** is shorthand when a lambda just calls an existing method: `String::length`, `System.out::println`, `Person::new`, `this::validate`.

Lambdas can read local variables from the enclosing scope only if they are **effectively final** — never reassigned. This prevents confusing shared mutable state; if you need to accumulate, use a stream reduction or a field instead.

Functional interfaces compose: `Predicate.and/or/negate`, `Function.andThen/compose`, `Comparator.thenComparing/reversed`. Annotate your own with `@FunctionalInterface` so the compiler enforces the single-abstract-method rule.
takeaways: A lambda implements a single-abstract-method interface
Know Function, Predicate, Consumer, Supplier and their compositions
Captured locals must be effectively final
pitfalls: Trying to increment a local counter inside a lambda — it won't compile because the variable must be effectively final.

quiz.q: Which functional interface matches `s -> s.isEmpty()` for a String s?
quiz.explain: It takes a String and returns a boolean, which is exactly Predicate<String>.test.

concepts.name: Streams
concepts.summary: Process collections declaratively with filter, map, sorted, collect, groupingBy and friends.
concepts.why: Streams express data transformations clearly and appear throughout modern Java codebases.
concepts.body:
A **stream** is a pipeline over a sequence of elements: a source, zero or more **intermediate operations**, and one **terminal operation**:

```java
List<String> result = orders.stream()        // source
    .filter(o -> o.total() > 100)               // intermediate
    .map(Order::customer)                       // intermediate
    .distinct()
    .sorted()
    .toList();                                  // terminal
```

Intermediate operations are **lazy**: nothing runs until the terminal operation pulls elements through, one at a time. That's why `filter(...).findFirst()` stops as soon as it finds a match.

Common operations:

- Intermediate: `filter`, `map`, `flatMap` (one-to-many), `distinct`, `sorted`, `limit`, `skip`, `peek` (debugging).
- Terminal: `toList()` (Java 16+, unmodifiable), `forEach`, `count`, `anyMatch`/`allMatch`, `findFirst`, `reduce`, `min`/`max`, and `collect`.

`Collectors` handles the richer cases: `groupingBy(Order::customer)` builds a `Map<K, List<V>>`, optionally with a downstream collector like `counting()` or `summingDouble(...)`; `toMap`, `joining(", ")`, and `partitioningBy`.

For primitives use `IntStream`, `mapToInt(...)`, `sum()`, `average()` — they avoid boxing. `IntStream.range(0, n)` replaces many index loops.

Rules to keep in mind:

- A stream can be consumed only once.
- Keep lambdas free of side effects; don't add to an external list from `forEach` — collect instead.
- `parallel()` is rarely a win for typical business code; measure before using it.

Streams are not always better than loops. If the pipeline needs complex state, early returns or checked exceptions, a plain loop is often clearer.
takeaways: source → lazy intermediate ops → one terminal op
`groupingBy`, `toMap`, `joining` and `partitioningBy` cover most aggregation needs
Use primitive streams for numbers; avoid side effects in lambdas
pitfalls: Reusing a stream after a terminal operation — it throws IllegalStateException.
Building results by mutating an outside list in `forEach` instead of collecting.

quiz.q: When does `list.stream().filter(x -> expensive(x))` call expensive()?
options: Only once a terminal operation runs
quiz.explain: Intermediate operations are lazy; work happens only when a terminal operation pulls elements.

quiz.q: Which collector turns a stream of orders into a Map from customer to list of orders?
quiz.explain: groupingBy classifies elements by a key function and collects each group into a list by default.

concepts.name: Optional
concepts.summary: Return Optional for values that may be absent and handle them with map, orElse, orElseThrow and ifPresent.
concepts.why: Optional makes "might be missing" visible in method signatures and cuts down on NullPointerExceptions.
concepts.body:
`Optional<T>` is a container that either holds a value or is empty. Its main job is as a **return type** for methods that may legitimately find nothing, such as `findUserByEmail`. The signature tells callers they must deal with absence, which a nullable return never does.

Create one with `Optional.of(value)` (value must be non-null), `Optional.ofNullable(maybeNull)`, or `Optional.empty()`. Streams return them from `findFirst`, `max`, `min` and `reduce`.

Consume it without unwrapping by hand:

- `map(f)` / `flatMap(f)` — transform the value if present.
- `filter(pred)` — keep the value only if it matches.
- `orElse(default)` — fallback value (always evaluated).
- `orElseGet(() -> compute())` — fallback computed lazily, only when empty.
- `orElseThrow()` — get the value or throw `NoSuchElementException`; `orElseThrow(() -> new NotFound(id))` for your own exception.
- `ifPresent(consumer)` and `ifPresentOrElse(consumer, runnable)`.

Calling `get()` after checking `isPresent()` works but is just null-checking with extra steps; the methods above are more expressive.

Guidelines the JDK designers recommend:

- Use Optional for return values, not for fields, method parameters or collection elements.
- Never return `null` from a method declared to return `Optional`.
- Return an empty collection rather than `Optional<List<T>>`.
- For primitives there are `OptionalInt`, `OptionalLong` and `OptionalDouble`.

Prefer `orElseGet` over `orElse` when the fallback is expensive, such as a database call — `orElse`'s argument is evaluated even when the value is present.
takeaways: Use Optional as a return type for "may be absent" results
Chain `map`/`filter` and finish with `orElse`, `orElseGet` or `orElseThrow`
Don't use Optional for fields or parameters, and never return null instead of one
pitfalls: Writing `if (opt.isPresent()) return opt.get();` everywhere — it's a null check in disguise.

quiz.q: Why prefer `orElseGet(() -> loadDefault())` over `orElse(loadDefault())`?
options: loadDefault() runs only when the Optional is empty
orElseGet is the only one that handles null
quiz.explain: orElse's argument is evaluated eagerly; orElseGet invokes the supplier only if needed.

concepts.name: Packages, Maven and Gradle
concepts.summary: Organise code into packages, understand the classpath and JARs, and build projects with Maven or Gradle.
concepts.why: Every real Java project uses packages and a build tool to compile, manage dependencies, test and package.
concepts.body:
A **package** groups related classes and gives them a namespace. Declare it at the top of the file (`package com.example.billing;`) and place the file in the matching directory, `com/example/billing/`. Package names are reversed domain names in lowercase. Use `import` to refer to classes from other packages by their simple name; `java.lang` is imported automatically.

At runtime the JVM finds classes on the **classpath**: a list of directories and **JAR** files (zip archives of `.class` files plus metadata). Managing that list by hand quickly becomes painful, which is why everyone uses a build tool.

**Maven** and **Gradle** both:

- download dependencies (and their transitive dependencies) from Maven Central by coordinates `groupId:artifactId:version`,
- use the standard layout: `src/main/java`, `src/main/resources`, `src/test/java`,
- compile, run tests and package a JAR with one command.

Maven is configured declaratively in `pom.xml` and runs lifecycle phases: `mvn package` compiles, tests and builds the JAR into `target/`. Gradle uses a Kotlin or Groovy build script (`build.gradle.kts`) and tasks: `./gradlew build` puts output in `build/`. Both projects normally commit a **wrapper** (`mvnw`, `gradlew`) so everyone uses the same tool version.

In Maven, dependency scope matters: `test` dependencies like JUnit are available only to tests. In Gradle the equivalent is `testImplementation` versus `implementation`.

Set the Java version explicitly — `<maven.compiler.release>21</maven.compiler.release>` in Maven, or a Java toolchain in Gradle — so builds don't depend on whichever JDK happens to be installed.
takeaways: Package names mirror directories: `com.example.app` → `com/example/app/`
Build tools resolve dependencies by group:artifact:version and use a standard layout
Commit the wrapper and pin the Java release for reproducible builds
pitfalls: Putting a file in a directory that doesn't match its package declaration, which leads to "class not found" errors.

quiz.q: In Maven, what does `<scope>test</scope>` on a dependency mean?
options: It is available to test code but not packaged with main code
It is downloaded only when tests fail
It replaces the main dependency during tests
It is ignored by the compiler
quiz.explain: Test-scoped dependencies are on the test classpath only, so production code can't use them.

concepts.name: Unit testing with JUnit 5
concepts.summary: Write and run JUnit 5 tests with assertions, assertThrows, lifecycle hooks and parameterized tests.
concepts.why: Automated tests let you change code with confidence, and JUnit is the standard testing framework in Java.
concepts.body:
**JUnit 5** (Jupiter) is the standard unit-testing framework. Tests live under `src/test/java`, in the same package as the code they test, and run with `mvn test` or `./gradlew test` (Gradle needs `useJUnitPlatform()` in its test task).

A test is a method annotated with `@Test`. It passes if it completes without throwing; assertions throw when expectations fail:

- `assertEquals(expected, actual)` — expected value first, so failure messages read correctly.
- `assertTrue`, `assertFalse`, `assertNull`, `assertNotNull`.
- `assertThrows(SomeException.class, () -> code())` returns the exception so you can check its message.
- `assertAll(...)` reports several failures at once instead of stopping at the first.

Test classes and methods don't need to be public in JUnit 5. `@BeforeEach` runs before every test (a fresh setup for each), and `@AfterEach` after. JUnit creates a new instance of the test class per test method, so tests don't share instance fields.

**Parameterized tests** run one test with many inputs: annotate with `@ParameterizedTest` and supply data with `@ValueSource`, `@CsvSource` or `@MethodSource`.

Good unit tests are fast, independent and deterministic. Structure each as arrange–act–assert, give it a name that states the behaviour (`rejectsNegativeAmounts`), and test one behaviour per method. Code against interfaces so you can pass simple fakes; libraries like Mockito and AssertJ (fluent assertions) are common additions.

Don't chase 100% coverage. Focus on logic with branches, edge cases (empty, null, boundaries) and bugs you have fixed, so they stay fixed.
takeaways: Annotate with `@Test`; put expected before actual in `assertEquals`
`assertThrows` checks error paths; `@ParameterizedTest` covers many inputs
Each test gets a fresh instance — keep tests independent and fast
pitfalls: Comparing doubles with `assertEquals(a, b)` without a delta and failing on rounding noise.

quiz.q: How does JUnit 5 treat instance fields of a test class between two @Test methods?
options: They are shared, so order matters
They are reset to null only if annotated
A new instance is created for each test method
quiz.explain: By default JUnit creates a fresh test class instance per test method, isolating instance state.

concepts.name: Generics in depth: wildcards and erasure
concepts.summary: Use bounded wildcards with the PECS rule, understand invariance and type erasure, and know what generics can't do at runtime.
concepts.why: Writing flexible library-style APIs — and decoding confusing compiler errors — needs a real model of how generics work.
concepts.body:
Generic types are **invariant**: even though `Integer` is a `Number`, a `List<Integer>` is *not* a `List<Number>`. If it were, you could add a `Double` to a list of integers through the `List<Number>` view. Wildcards restore flexibility safely:

- `List<? extends Number>` — a list of *some* subtype of Number. You can read elements as `Number`, but can't add (except `null`), because the exact type is unknown.
- `List<? super Integer>` — a list of Integer or a supertype. You can add `Integer`s, but reading only gives you `Object`.
- `List<?>` — any list; read as `Object`.

The rule of thumb is **PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super**. A parameter you read from is a producer (`extends`); one you write into is a consumer (`super`). That's why `Collections.copy` is declared `copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)`, and why comparator parameters are usually `Comparator<? super T>`.

Generics are implemented by **type erasure**: the compiler checks types, then erases type parameters to their bounds (usually `Object`) and inserts casts. At runtime a `List<String>` and a `List<Integer>` are the same class. Consequences:

- No `new T()`, no `new T[n]`, no `instanceof List<String>` — pass a `Class<T>` or a `Supplier<T>` when you need to create instances.
- You can't overload `m(List<String>)` and `m(List<Integer>)`; they erase to the same signature.
- Mixing generics with arrays or raw types leads to **heap pollution** and "unchecked" warnings. Treat those warnings as bugs unless you can prove safety, then suppress narrowly with `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")`.

Use wildcards in method parameters, not in return types — callers shouldn't have to deal with them.
takeaways: Generic types are invariant: `List<Integer>` is not a `List<Number>`
PECS — read from `? extends T`, write into `? super T`
Type parameters are erased at runtime: no `new T()`, no `instanceof List<String>`
pitfalls: Returning wildcard types from public methods, forcing every caller to handle them.

quiz.q: Which call compiles for a method `void addAll(List<? super Integer> sink)`?
quiz.explain: List<Number> is a list of a supertype of Integer, which is what ? super Integer allows.

quiz.q: Why can't you write `new T[10]` in a generic class?
options: Generic classes can't use arrays at all
T is erased, so the runtime doesn't know which array type to create
quiz.explain: Arrays need their exact component type at runtime, but erasure removes T.

concepts.name: Sealed types and pattern matching
concepts.summary: Model closed hierarchies with sealed interfaces and records, then destructure them with instanceof and switch patterns.
concepts.why: Java 21's pattern matching makes data-oriented code concise and lets the compiler prove you handled every case.
takeaways: `sealed ... permits` closes a hierarchy so the compiler knows all subtypes
Record patterns destructure; `when` guards refine a case
Switches over sealed types are exhaustive — new subtypes cause compile errors, not runtime bugs
pitfalls: Putting a general case (e.g. `case Rect r`) before a guarded, more specific one — the compiler rejects the dominated case.

quiz.q: A `switch` over a sealed interface covers every permitted record. What happens when a new permitted record is added?
options: It falls into an implicit default
The switch fails to compile until the new type is handled
quiz.explain: Exhaustiveness is checked against the permits list, so the missing case is a compile error.

concepts.name: Threads and thread safety
concepts.summary: Start threads, recognise race conditions, and fix them with synchronized, locks, atomics and concurrent collections.
concepts.why: Servers, UIs and batch jobs all run code concurrently, and race conditions are among the hardest bugs to find.
concepts.body:
A **thread** is an independent path of execution within the JVM; all threads share the same heap. You can start one with `Thread.ofPlatform().start(runnable)` or `new Thread(runnable).start()`, and wait for it with `join()`. In practice you'll usually submit tasks to an executor (next lesson), but the safety rules are the same.

When threads share **mutable state**, you get **race conditions**. `count++` looks atomic but is three steps — read, add, write — and two threads can interleave them so an increment is lost. Worse, without synchronization one thread may never *see* another's writes (more on that in the memory-model lesson).

Tools, from simplest to most specialised:

- **Don't share** mutable state: confine data to one thread, or use immutable objects (records, `List.copyOf`).
- **synchronized** — a method or block that only one thread at a time can run per lock object; it also makes writes visible to the next thread that takes the same lock.
- **java.util.concurrent.atomic** — `AtomicInteger`, `AtomicLong`, `LongAdder` for counters and lock-free updates.
- **Concurrent collections** — `ConcurrentHashMap` (with atomic `merge`, `compute`), `CopyOnWriteArrayList`, `BlockingQueue` for producer-consumer.
- **ReentrantLock** and `ReadWriteLock` when you need timeouts, try-lock or fairness.

Guard **compound actions** too: `if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v)` is racy even on a ConcurrentHashMap — use `putIfAbsent` or `computeIfAbsent`.

Keep critical sections short, never call unknown code while holding a lock, and always acquire multiple locks in the same order to avoid **deadlock**.
takeaways: Shared mutable state + no synchronization = race condition
Prefer immutability and confinement; then atomics and concurrent collections; then locks
Make compound actions atomic (`merge`, `computeIfAbsent`), not check-then-act
pitfalls: Assuming `count++` or `HashMap` is safe to use from several threads.
Acquiring two locks in different orders in different places, causing deadlock.

quiz.q: Why can `counter++` on a shared int lose updates?
options: It is a read-modify-write sequence that threads can interleave
quiz.explain: Two threads can both read the same old value and write back the same incremented value.

concepts.name: Executors and thread pools
concepts.summary: Submit tasks to an ExecutorService, collect results with Future, and shut pools down correctly.
concepts.why: Executors separate what to run from how to run it, and are the standard way to do concurrent work in Java.
concepts.body:
Creating raw threads for every task is expensive and unmanageable. An **ExecutorService** accepts tasks and runs them on threads it manages:

- `submit(Runnable)` or `submit(Callable<T>)` returns a **Future<T>**; `future.get()` blocks until the result is ready and rethrows a task failure wrapped in `ExecutionException`.
- `invokeAll(tasks)` runs a collection of callables and waits for all of them.
- `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n)` suits CPU-bound work with `n` near `Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()`.
- `Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(n)` runs tasks after a delay or periodically.
- `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` (Java 21) is the modern choice for I/O-bound tasks — see the virtual threads lesson.

An executor must be **shut down**, or its non-daemon threads keep the JVM alive. Since Java 19 `ExecutorService` is `AutoCloseable`: in a try-with-resources block, `close()` stops accepting tasks and waits for submitted ones to finish. In older code you'll see `shutdown()` followed by `awaitTermination(...)`.

`Future.get()` has an overload with a timeout — use it whenever a stuck task shouldn't hang the caller. `cancel(true)` interrupts a running task; tasks cooperate by checking `Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()` or by letting blocking calls throw `InterruptedException`.

Handle `InterruptedException` properly: either propagate it or restore the flag with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()`. Swallowing it breaks cancellation.

Beware unbounded queues: a fixed pool fed faster than it drains will queue tasks until memory runs out. For production servers, use `ThreadPoolExecutor` with a bounded queue and a rejection policy, or limit concurrency with a `Semaphore`.
takeaways: Submit tasks to an `ExecutorService` instead of creating threads by hand
Always shut executors down — try-with-resources does it in Java 19+
Use timeouts on `Future.get` and never swallow `InterruptedException`
pitfalls: Forgetting to shut down an executor, so the application never exits.

quiz.q: A task submitted with `submit(callable)` throws an exception. What does `future.get()` do?
options: Nothing; the exception is logged and lost
Throws ExecutionException wrapping the original exception
quiz.explain: Future.get rethrows task failures wrapped in ExecutionException; getCause() gives the original.

concepts.name: CompletableFuture
concepts.summary: Compose asynchronous steps with thenApply, thenCompose, thenCombine, allOf and exceptionally instead of blocking on futures.
concepts.why: Calling several services concurrently and combining their results is a core backend task, and CompletableFuture is Java's standard tool for it.
concepts.body:
A plain `Future` only lets you block with `get()`. **CompletableFuture** lets you describe what should happen *when* a result arrives, building a pipeline of dependent steps.

Start work with `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(supplier, executor)` (or `runAsync` for no result). Without an executor argument it uses the shared `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()`, which is sized for CPU work — pass your own executor for blocking I/O.

Then chain:

- `thenApply(fn)` — transform the result (like `map`).
- `thenCompose(fn)` — the function itself returns a CompletableFuture; flatten it (like `flatMap`). Use it to chain dependent async calls.
- `thenCombine(other, (a, b) -> ...)` — combine two independent futures.
- `thenAccept(consumer)` — consume the result at the end.
- `allOf(f1, f2, ...)` — completes when all complete; then read each with `join()`. `anyOf` completes on the first.

Errors propagate down the chain, skipping normal stages, until handled with `exceptionally(ex -> fallback)` or `handle((value, ex) -> ...)`. The exception you receive is usually a `CompletionException` wrapping the real cause. `orTimeout(...)` and `completeOnTimeout(value, ...)` add deadlines.

At the edge of your program, `join()` waits and throws unchecked `CompletionException`; `get()` throws checked exceptions.

Each stage runs on whichever thread completed the previous stage, or the caller's thread if it was already complete. The `...Async` variants (`thenApplyAsync`) hop to an executor explicitly.

With virtual threads (Java 21), plain blocking code in many threads is often simpler than long async chains. CompletableFuture remains valuable for composing results and for APIs that already return futures, such as `HttpClient.sendAsync`.
takeaways: `thenApply` maps, `thenCompose` chains async calls, `thenCombine` joins two
Handle failures with `exceptionally` or `handle`; they arrive wrapped in CompletionException
Pass your own executor for blocking I/O instead of using the common pool
pitfalls: Calling `join()` right after each `supplyAsync`, which makes the calls sequential again.

quiz.q: You have `CompletableFuture<User> u` and a method `CompletableFuture<List<Order>> ordersOf(User)`. Which gives a `CompletableFuture<List<Order>>`?
quiz.explain: thenApply would produce a nested future; thenCompose flattens a function that returns a CompletableFuture.

concepts.name: Virtual threads
concepts.summary: Use Java 21 virtual threads to run huge numbers of blocking tasks cheaply, and know their pitfalls: pinning, pooling and ThreadLocals.
concepts.why: Virtual threads let plain, readable blocking code scale like async code — the biggest change to Java concurrency in years.
concepts.body:
A traditional **platform thread** is a thin wrapper over an operating-system thread: each costs around a megabyte of stack and a kernel scheduling slot, so servers top out at a few thousand. A request that spends most of its time waiting on a database or HTTP call holds that scarce thread the whole time.

A **virtual thread** (final in Java 21) is managed by the JVM. It runs on a small pool of **carrier** platform threads, and when it blocks on I/O, a lock or `sleep`, the JVM unmounts it and frees the carrier for another virtual thread. You can have millions of them.

Creating them:

- `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` — one new virtual thread per task.
- `Thread.ofVirtual().start(runnable)` or `Thread.startVirtualThread(runnable)`.

The programming model is ordinary blocking code: write `var body = client.send(request, ...)`, not callbacks. Stack traces, debuggers and profilers work as usual.

Guidelines:

- **Don't pool** virtual threads. They are cheap; create one per task. To limit concurrency against a fragile resource, use a `Semaphore`, not a small pool.
- They help **I/O-bound** workloads with many concurrent tasks. CPU-bound work gains nothing — there are still only as many cores.
- In Java 21, blocking inside a `synchronized` block **pins** the virtual thread to its carrier, so frequent long blocking under `synchronized` can starve the carriers. Prefer `ReentrantLock` around blocking calls on Java 21; JDK 24 removed most pinning.
- Be careful with `ThreadLocal` caches of expensive objects — with a million threads you get a million copies.

Frameworks such as Spring Boot, Helidon and Quarkus can run request handling on virtual threads with a configuration switch.
takeaways: Virtual threads are cheap JVM-managed threads that unmount while blocked
Create one per task; limit access to resources with a Semaphore, not a pool
On Java 21, avoid long blocking inside `synchronized` (pinning); use `ReentrantLock`
pitfalls: Using virtual threads for CPU-heavy computation and expecting a speed-up.

quiz.q: What happens when a virtual thread blocks on a socket read (outside synchronized)?
options: The JVM unmounts it so the carrier can run other virtual threads
Its carrier OS thread blocks too
It is converted to a platform thread
quiz.explain: Blocking I/O parks the virtual thread and frees the carrier for other work.

quiz.q: You need at most 20 concurrent calls to a rate-limited API from virtual threads. Best tool?
options: A fixed pool of 20 virtual threads
quiz.explain: Virtual threads shouldn't be pooled; a Semaphore limits concurrency directly.

concepts.name: Annotations and reflection
concepts.summary: Declare and read custom annotations, inspect and invoke code at runtime with reflection, and know the costs.
concepts.why: Frameworks like Spring, JUnit, Jackson and Hibernate are built on annotations and reflection; understanding them demystifies the magic.
concepts.body:
An **annotation** attaches metadata to code. Some are for the compiler (`@Override`, `@Deprecated`, `@SuppressWarnings`, `@FunctionalInterface`); most in real projects are read by frameworks (`@Test`, `@Entity`, `@GetMapping`).

Declaring one uses `@interface`, with two meta-annotations that matter:

- `@Retention` — `SOURCE` (discarded by the compiler), `CLASS` (in the class file, the default) or `RUNTIME` (readable via reflection — what frameworks need).
- `@Target` — where it may appear: `TYPE`, `METHOD`, `FIELD`, `PARAMETER`, and more.

Annotation elements look like methods and can have defaults: `String value() default "";`. An element named `value` can be set without a name: `@Route("/home")`.

**Reflection** (`java.lang.reflect`) lets code inspect classes at runtime. Starting from a `Class<?>` object (`obj.getClass()`, `Foo.class`, `Class.forName(name)`), you can list `getDeclaredMethods()`, `getDeclaredFields()` and constructors, read annotations with `getAnnotation(...)`, and call `method.invoke(target, args)` or `constructor.newInstance(...)`. Exceptions thrown by the invoked method arrive wrapped in `InvocationTargetException`.

Costs and limits:

- It bypasses compile-time checks: typos in names fail at runtime.
- It is slower than direct calls (though the JIT and `MethodHandle`s narrow the gap).
- `setAccessible(true)` on private members is blocked across module boundaries unless the package is **opened** — the module system enforces strong encapsulation of JDK internals.

Use reflection to build frameworks and tooling, not in everyday business logic. Annotation processors offer a compile-time alternative that generates code (Lombok, MapStruct, Dagger).
takeaways: Frameworks need `@Retention(RUNTIME)` annotations to see them via reflection
Reflection inspects and invokes members at runtime, trading safety and speed for flexibility
The module system blocks deep reflection into packages that aren't opened
pitfalls: Forgetting `@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)`, so `getAnnotation` always returns null.

quiz.q: A custom annotation has no @Retention. Can a framework read it with getAnnotation at runtime?
options: No, the default CLASS retention isn't visible to reflection
quiz.explain: The default retention is CLASS: stored in the class file but not exposed through reflection.

concepts.name: Files and I/O with NIO.2
concepts.summary: Read and write files with Path and Files, stream large files line by line, walk directories, and handle charsets correctly.
concepts.why: Almost every application reads configuration, writes reports or processes data files.
concepts.body:
Modern file handling uses **NIO.2** (`java.nio.file`). A **Path** represents a location: `Path.of("data", "input.csv")` builds it portably, and `resolve`, `getParent`, `getFileName` and `normalize` manipulate it without touching the disk.

The **Files** utility class does the actual I/O:

- Small files: `Files.readString(path)`, `Files.readAllLines(path)`, `Files.writeString(path, text)` and `Files.write(path, lines)`.
- Large files: `Files.lines(path)` returns a lazy `Stream<String>`; `Files.newBufferedReader` and `newBufferedWriter` give classic readers and writers.
- Management: `exists`, `createDirectories`, `copy`, `move` (with options like `REPLACE_EXISTING`, `ATOMIC_MOVE`), `delete`, `deleteIfExists`, `size`.
- Directories: `Files.list(dir)` for one level, `Files.walk(dir)` recursively, `Files.find` with a filter.

Streams returned by `lines`, `list` and `walk` hold open file handles, so always use them in **try-with-resources**. Forgetting this leaks descriptors and eventually fails with "Too many open files".

Text needs a **charset**. Since Java 18 the default is UTF-8 everywhere (JEP 400), and the `Files` methods use UTF-8 unless told otherwise. Pass a charset explicitly when reading files from other systems, for example `StandardCharsets.ISO_8859_1`.

Write options control behaviour: `StandardOpenOption.APPEND`, `CREATE`, `TRUNCATE_EXISTING`. To avoid readers seeing half-written files, write to a temporary file in the same directory and `move` it into place with `ATOMIC_MOVE`.

You'll still meet `java.io.File` and `InputStream`/`OutputStream` in older APIs; `file.toPath()` and `path.toFile()` bridge the two worlds.
takeaways: Use `Path.of` and the `Files` utility methods for file I/O
Close `Files.lines`, `list` and `walk` streams with try-with-resources
UTF-8 is the default since Java 18; specify charsets for foreign files
pitfalls: Using `Files.readAllLines` on multi-gigabyte files and running out of memory — stream them instead.

quiz.q: Why should `Files.lines(path)` be used in try-with-resources?
options: It is required by the compiler
Otherwise lines are returned in random order
The stream holds an open file handle that must be closed
quiz.explain: The lazy stream keeps the file open until closed; leaking it exhausts file descriptors.

concepts.name: The module system (JPMS)
concepts.summary: Describe modules with module-info.java: requires, exports, opens and transitive, and build small runtimes with jlink.
concepts.why: Modules give strong encapsulation for libraries and the JDK itself, and explain the access errors you meet on modern Java.
takeaways: `module-info.java` declares `requires`, `exports` and `opens`
Unexported packages are inaccessible, even for public classes
Classpath code runs in the unnamed module; JDK internals are closed to reflection by default
pitfalls: Silencing reflective-access errors with blanket `--add-opens` flags instead of upgrading the offending library.

quiz.q: A framework must use reflection on private fields in your package but other modules shouldn't compile against it. What do you declare?
quiz.explain: opens grants runtime deep reflection without exporting the package's types for compilation.

concepts.name: Java Memory Model and happens-before
concepts.summary: Understand visibility, reordering and the happens-before rules that make volatile, synchronized and final fields work.
concepts.why: Concurrent code that "works on my machine" can fail on another CPU or JIT; the memory model tells you what is actually guaranteed.
concepts.body:
Compilers, the JIT and CPUs all **reorder** and cache memory operations for speed. Within one thread you can't tell; across threads you can. The **Java Memory Model** (JLS chapter 17) defines which writes another thread is guaranteed to see.

The central idea is **happens-before**. If action A happens-before action B, then B sees A's effects (and everything before A). Key rules:

- Program order: each action in a thread happens-before later actions in that thread.
- Monitor lock: unlocking a monitor happens-before every later lock of the *same* monitor.
- `volatile`: a write to a volatile field happens-before every subsequent read of that field.
- `Thread.start()` happens-before the started thread's actions; a thread's actions happen-before another thread returns from `join()` on it.
- Transitivity ties them together. `java.util.concurrent` classes document their own edges (e.g. putting into a `BlockingQueue` happens-before taking it out).
