Two conflicting accesses (at least one a write) not ordered by happens-before form a **data race**, and the reading thread may see stale values indefinitely. A classic failure: a `boolean running` flag polled in a loop without `volatile` — the JIT may hoist the read out of the loop and spin forever.

`volatile` gives visibility and ordering but not atomicity: `volatile int x; x++` is still racy. Use atomics for that.

**final fields** have a special guarantee: if the object reference doesn't escape during construction, every thread sees the final fields' constructed values without synchronization. That is what makes immutable objects safe to share.

Double-checked locking for lazy singletons works only if the field is `volatile`; the simpler alternative is the holder-class idiom, which relies on the class-initialization guarantee.
takeaways: Without a happens-before edge, another thread may see stale or reordered values
Edges come from locks, volatile, thread start/join and java.util.concurrent classes
`volatile` gives visibility, not atomicity; final fields make safe immutable objects
pitfalls: Polling a non-volatile flag from another thread, which can loop forever after JIT optimisation.
Double-checked locking without `volatile` on the instance field.

quiz.q: Thread A writes `data = 42` and then writes volatile `ready = true`. Thread B reads `ready == true`, then reads `data`. What does B see?
options: 42 — guaranteed by the volatile happens-before edge
Whatever is in its CPU cache
quiz.explain: The volatile write happens-before the read that sees it, and program order carries the earlier data write along.

quiz.q: Which is still a data race?
options: Reading a final field of a properly constructed immutable object
Accessing a field only inside synchronized blocks on the same lock
Incrementing a volatile int from two threads
quiz.explain: volatile ensures visibility, but x++ is a read-modify-write that two threads can interleave.

concepts.name: Garbage collection and the heap
concepts.summary: How the JVM reclaims memory: reachability, generations, G1, ZGC and Parallel collectors, heap sizing and memory leaks.
concepts.why: Latency spikes, OutOfMemoryErrors and container memory limits all come down to understanding the heap and the collector.
concepts.body:
Objects live on the **heap**; local variables and call frames live on per-thread **stacks**. An object is eligible for collection when it is no longer **reachable** from GC roots — thread stacks, static fields, JNI references. Cycles don't matter; reachability does.

Most collectors are **generational**, based on the observation that most objects die young. New objects go to the young generation, collected often and cheaply by copying the few survivors; objects that survive several collections are promoted to the old generation, collected less often.

HotSpot collectors in Java 21:

- **G1** (default) — divides the heap into regions, collects mostly concurrently, aims at a pause-time goal (`-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis`, default 200 ms). A good default for most services.
- **ZGC** (`-XX:+UseZGC`) — almost fully concurrent, pauses typically under a millisecond regardless of heap size. Java 21 added generational ZGC via `-XX:+ZGenerational`, which later became the only mode.
- **Parallel** (`-XX:+UseParallelGC`) — maximum throughput with longer stop-the-world pauses; good for batch jobs.
- **Serial** — single-threaded, for tiny heaps and small containers.

Size the heap with `-Xmx` / `-Xms`, or in containers with `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75`. Leave headroom: thread stacks, metaspace, code cache and direct buffers live outside the heap.

A Java **memory leak** is an object kept reachable by accident: an ever-growing static map or cache, listeners never removed, ThreadLocals on pooled threads. The symptom is old-generation usage that climbs after each collection until `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`. Use `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` and analyse the dump's dominator tree to find what holds the memory.

Turn on GC logging in production with `-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log` — it's cheap and invaluable.
takeaways: Objects are collected when unreachable from GC roots — cycles don't leak
G1 is the default; ZGC for very low latency, Parallel for throughput
Leaks are accidental references (static maps, listeners, ThreadLocals); diagnose with heap dumps and GC logs
pitfalls: Setting `-Xmx` equal to the container memory limit, leaving no room for non-heap memory and getting OOM-killed.

quiz.q: Two objects reference each other but nothing else references either. What happens?
quiz.explain: Java's tracing collectors use reachability from roots, so unreachable cycles are collected.

quiz.q: A latency-sensitive service with a 32 GB heap suffers 300 ms pauses. Which change is most likely to help?
quiz.explain: ZGC does nearly all work concurrently and keeps pauses sub-millisecond independent of heap size.

concepts.name: Bytecode and javap
concepts.summary: Read the JVM's stack-based bytecode with javap, and see how method calls, lambdas and string concatenation really compile.
concepts.why: Reading bytecode settles debates about what the compiler actually generates and is the foundation for agents, profilers and code generation.
concepts.body:
`javac` compiles to **bytecode**, the instruction set of the JVM. Inspect it with `javap -c -p MyClass.class` (`-v` adds the constant pool and more).

The JVM is a **stack machine**. Each method frame has an array of **local variable slots** (slot 0 is `this` in instance methods) and an **operand stack**. `a + b` for ints becomes `iload_1`, `iload_2`, `iadd`, `istore_3`. Instruction prefixes encode types: `i` int, `l` long, `d` double, `a` reference.

Method calls come in five flavours, and knowing them explains a lot of language behaviour:

- `invokestatic` — static methods.
- `invokevirtual` — ordinary instance methods, dispatched on the runtime class (polymorphism).
- `invokeinterface` — calls through an interface type.
- `invokespecial` — constructors (`<init>`) and `super.` calls: no dynamic dispatch. (Since Java 11, calls to private methods use `invokevirtual`, a side effect of nestmates.)
- `invokedynamic` — the call site is linked at runtime by a bootstrap method. Lambdas use it (via `LambdaMetafactory`), and so does string concatenation since Java 9 (`StringConcatFactory`).

Other details become visible too: generics are erased to their bounds with `checkcast` inserted at use sites; autoboxing turns into `Integer.valueOf` and `intValue()` calls; a `switch` on strings becomes a `hashCode` lookup followed by `equals`; constructors and static initializers appear as `<init>` and `<clinit>`.

The class file also carries the **constant pool** (names, literals, method references), a version number (65 for Java 21) and attributes such as line number tables that power stack traces.

Libraries like ASM and ByteBuddy generate and rewrite bytecode — that's how Mockito, Hibernate proxies and Java agents work. A standard Class-File API arrived as a preview after Java 21.
takeaways: The JVM is a stack machine: locals in slots, work on an operand stack
invokestatic, invokevirtual, invokeinterface, invokespecial and invokedynamic encode call semantics
Lambdas and string concatenation are linked at runtime through invokedynamic
pitfalls: Assuming source-level features like generics exist at runtime — `javap` shows they're erased to casts.

quiz.q: An override calls `super.toString()`. Which instruction does javac emit for that call?
quiz.explain: super calls must bypass dynamic dispatch to reach the parent's implementation, so they use invokespecial.

quiz.q: How is a lambda expression implemented in bytecode?
options: As a separate anonymous .class file generated by javac
As an invokedynamic call site whose bootstrap creates the functional object at runtime
As a static field initialised in <clinit>
quiz.explain: javac emits the body as a private method and an invokedynamic site bootstrapped by LambdaMetafactory.

concepts.name: Class loading and initialization
concepts.summary: Follow a class through loading, linking and initialization; understand the loader hierarchy, delegation and NoClassDefFoundError.
concepts.why: Classpath conflicts, plugin systems, application servers and startup time all hinge on how classes are loaded.
concepts.body:
The JVM loads classes **lazily**, the first time they are needed. Each class goes through three phases (JVMS chapter 5):

- **Loading** — a class loader finds the bytes (from a JAR, directory, network, or generated) and creates a `Class` object.
- **Linking** — *verification* checks the bytecode is type-safe and well-formed; *preparation* allocates static fields with default values; *resolution* turns symbolic references into direct ones, often lazily.
- **Initialization** — runs the static initializer `<clinit>`: static field assignments and `static { }` blocks, in source order. It happens on first active use (creating an instance, calling a static method, reading a non-constant static field) and is guaranteed to run exactly once, thread-safely.

Class loaders form a hierarchy: the **bootstrap** loader (core `java.base` classes), the **platform** loader (other JDK modules), and the **application** (system) loader (your classpath or module path). Loaders use **parent delegation**: ask the parent first, and only load the class yourself if the parent can't. That stops applications from replacing `java.lang.String`.

A class's runtime identity is its name **plus its defining loader**. The same class loaded by two loaders gives two distinct types — the source of baffling `ClassCastException: Foo cannot be cast to Foo` in app servers and plugin systems.

Know the two errors apart:

- `ClassNotFoundException` — a checked exception from explicit loading (`Class.forName`) when the class can't be found.
- `NoClassDefFoundError` — the class was present at compile time but is missing at runtime, *or* its static initializer previously failed (the first attempt throws `ExceptionInInitializerError`).

Startup time is dominated by loading and verifying classes. **Class Data Sharing** (CDS, on by default for JDK classes; `-XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit` for your app) maps pre-parsed classes from an archive to speed it up.
takeaways: Classes are loaded lazily: load, link (verify, prepare, resolve), initialize
Loaders delegate to their parent first; class identity = name + defining loader
NoClassDefFoundError means missing at runtime or a previously failed static initializer
pitfalls: Throwing from a static initializer: the first use gets ExceptionInInitializerError, every later use NoClassDefFoundError.

quiz.q: Reading `Config.NAME`, where `static final String NAME = "app";`, from another class:
options: Throws if Config isn't loaded yet
Loads Config with a new class loader
Does not initialize Config, because the constant is inlined at compile time
quiz.explain: Compile-time constants are copied into the using class's constant pool, so no initialization is triggered.

concepts.name: JIT compilation and warm-up
concepts.summary: How HotSpot interprets, profiles and compiles hot code with C1 and C2: inlining, escape analysis, deoptimization and warm-up.
concepts.why: JIT behaviour explains why Java gets faster after startup, why naive benchmarks lie, and which code shapes run fast.
concepts.body:
HotSpot starts by **interpreting** bytecode while collecting a **profile**: how often each method and loop runs, which branches are taken, which concrete types appear at each call site. Hot code is then compiled to native machine code by the **JIT** (just-in-time compiler). With **tiered compilation** (the default):

- **C1** compiles quickly with light optimisation, so code speeds up soon after startup.
- **C2** later recompiles the hottest methods with aggressive, profile-guided optimisation.

Key optimisations:

- **Inlining** — copying a callee's body into the caller. It is the gateway to every other optimisation. Small methods and getters cost nothing once inlined, so write clear small methods.
- **Devirtualization** — if a call site has only ever seen one or two receiver types (monomorphic or bimorphic), C2 inlines them behind a cheap type check. Megamorphic sites (many types) stay as slower virtual calls.
- **Escape analysis** — if an object never escapes a method, C2 can eliminate its allocation and keep fields in registers.
- Loop optimisations: range-check elimination, unrolling and auto-vectorisation.

These optimisations are **speculative**. If an assumption breaks — a new subclass gets loaded, or a never-taken branch is taken — the JVM **deoptimizes**: it discards the compiled code, falls back to the interpreter and recompiles later.

Consequences: a JVM application needs **warm-up** before reaching peak speed, so measure after warm-up and use JMH for microbenchmarks, which also defeats dead-code elimination. `-XX:+PrintCompilation` shows methods as they are compiled, and JFR records compilation and deoptimization events. For startup-sensitive workloads, CDS archives, Project Leyden work and GraalVM native image move work ahead of time.
takeaways: Code runs interpreted first; hot methods are compiled by C1, then C2 using profiles
Inlining enables everything else; small methods are effectively free

concepts.name: Performance tuning and profiling
concepts.summary: Find real bottlenecks with JFR, JDK Mission Control, jcmd and JMH, and fix the usual suspects: allocation, locks, I/O and GC.
concepts.why: Guessing at performance problems wastes time; measuring with the JDK's own tools finds the actual cause quickly.
concepts.body:
The first rule of performance work is **measure, don't guess**. Define the target (p99 latency, throughput, memory), reproduce the problem under realistic load, then profile.

The JDK ships excellent tools:

- **JDK Flight Recorder (JFR)** — a low-overhead event recorder built into the JVM, safe to run in production. Start it with `-XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=60s,filename=rec.jfr`, or attach to a running process with `jcmd <pid> JFR.start`. It records CPU samples, allocations, GC pauses, lock contention, I/O and thread states.
- **JDK Mission Control (JMC)** — the GUI for analysing `.jfr` files; the `jfr` CLI (`jfr print`, `jfr summary`) works too.
- **jcmd** — the Swiss army knife: `Thread.print` (thread dump), `GC.heap_info`, `GC.heap_dump`, `VM.flags`, `VM.native_memory`.
- External profilers such as async-profiler produce flame graphs of CPU and allocation.

For small pieces of code, use **JMH** (Java Microbenchmark Harness). It handles warm-up, forks fresh JVMs, and prevents the JIT from eliminating or hoisting the code under test — pitfalls that make hand-written timing loops meaningless.

Typical findings and fixes:

- **Allocation pressure** — boxing in hot loops, needless copies and string concatenation in loops drive GC. Use primitives, reuse buffers, presize collections.
- **Lock contention** — JFR's monitor events point at hot locks; reduce the scope, use concurrent structures, or avoid sharing.
- **I/O waits** — batch calls, add caching or connection pooling, or use virtual threads to overlap waiting.
- **GC** — check GC logs for pause times and frequency before reaching for flags; often the fix is allocating less or sizing the heap correctly.

Change one thing at a time, re-measure, and keep the benchmark so regressions are caught later.
takeaways: Measure first: reproduce, profile, change one thing, re-measure
JFR + JMC and jcmd are built in and safe for production diagnostics
Use JMH for microbenchmarks — hand-written timing loops lie
pitfalls: Tuning JVM flags before profiling, when the real problem is allocation or contention in application code.

quiz.q: Why is JMH preferred over timing a loop with System.nanoTime()?
options: JMH handles warm-up, forking and prevents JIT dead-code elimination from skewing results
JMH runs code in the interpreter for fairness
quiz.explain: Without those controls the JIT can optimise away or hoist the measured code and warm-up distorts timings.
